grammar.title: Follow the narrator’s explanatory ending
grammar.formation: Plain verb / i-adjective clause + のです／のでした; noun / na stem + なのです. The source 匂がするのでした ends the explanation; it is not causal ので + a following main clause.
grammar.explanation: The narrator frames an observation as something the reader should now understand. Recognise the clause before の and the final でした. Earlier んです returns in a literary narrative; this is not a newly invented N1-only form.
grammar.example: 香水だと思った。ところが、酢の匂いがするのでした。
grammar.translation: They thought it was perfume. Yet it turned out to smell of vinegar.

examples.ja: {香水|こうすい}だと{思|おも}った。ところが、{酢|す}の{匂|にお}いがするのでした。
examples.en: They thought it was perfume. Yet it turned out to smell of vinegar.

examples.ja: {二人|ふたり}は{寒|さむ}さの{予防|よぼう}だと{思|おも}っていたのです。
examples.en: The two men thought it was to prevent chapping in the cold.

examples.ja: {怖|こわ}かったのは、{最後|さいご}の{注文|ちゅうもん}なのです。
examples.en: It was the last instruction that frightened them.

grammar.mistake: Do not translate every sentence-final のでした as “because” and invent an absent following result.

grammar.title: Recover an expectation before ところが
grammar.formation: Sentence A。ところが、observed or established unexpected result B。 Distinguish independent connector from verb + たところが.
grammar.explanation: Find the earlier expectation and the actual discovery. Here perfume should have a perfume scent, but it smells like vinegar. Merely comparing two unrelated preferences does not supply this reversal.
grammar.example: 香水をつけた。ところが、酢くさい。
grammar.translation: They put on perfume, but it smells of vinegar.

examples.ja: {香水|こうすい}をつけた。ところが、{酢|す}くさい。
examples.en: They put on perfume, but it smells of vinegar.

examples.ja: {扉|とびら}を{押|お}した。ところが、{動|うご}かなかった。
examples.en: He pushed the door, but it wouldn’t move.

examples.ja: {安心|あんしん}した。ところが、また{注文|ちゅうもん}があった。
examples.en: They felt relieved, but there was another instruction.

grammar.mistake: ところが introduces an established surprise here, not a new request or a speaker’s unfulfilled plan. It is not the topic shift ところで.

grammar.title: Find the recipient of a polite instruction
grammar.formation: Verb te-form + ください; お + appropriate verb masu stem + ください, e.g. 待つ→お待ちください. ご + compatible Sino-Japanese action noun + ください is also possible.
grammar.explanation: A polite form still tells someone to do something. Identify the recipient and object: the written instruction asks the gentlemen to put cream on their own bodies. Politeness does not establish a benevolent motive. The ぬれ quotation recalls the plain imperative 塗れ.
grammar.example: 壺のクリームを手に塗ってください。
grammar.translation: Put the cream from the jar on your hands, please.

examples.ja: {壺|つぼ}のクリームを{手|て}に{塗|ぬ}ってください。
examples.en: Put the cream from the jar on your hands, please.

examples.ja: {次|つぎ}の{扉|とびら}の{前|まえ}でお{待|ま}ちください。
examples.en: Please wait in front of the next door.

examples.ja: {文|ぶん}の{終|お}わりをご{確認|かくにん}ください。
examples.en: Please check the end of the sentence.

grammar.mistake: お + te-form + ください is not this pattern. ご確認ください is valid; do not extend the pattern to every verb or infer goodwill from polite wording.

grammar.title: Keep the eater and the food distinct
grammar.formation: 食べる→食べさせる: Xが人に料理を食べさせる. Result construction: Xが人を料理にする. Passive 食べられる and potential 食べられる require context, not sound alone.
grammar.explanation: The source contrasts letting the visitors eat dishes with turning the visitors into dishes. In the first half 人に is the eater and 料理を the food; in the second 人を is what is transformed. The sign’s たべられます sounds reassuring before the later reversal.
grammar.example: 店は客に料理を食べさせる。
grammar.translation: The restaurant has the guests eat food.

examples.ja: {店|みせ}は{客|きゃく}に{料理|りょうり}を{食|た}べさせる。
examples.en: The restaurant has the guests eat food.

examples.ja: {店|みせ}は{客|きゃく}を{料理|りょうり}にする。
examples.en: The restaurant turns the guests into food.

examples.ja: この{文|ぶん}では、{客|きゃく}が{食|た}べるのではなく、{客|きゃく}が{食|た}べられる。
examples.en: In this sentence, the guests don’t eat; they are eaten.

grammar.mistake: 食べさせる does not mean “be eaten.” The same 食べられる form may be potential or passive; identify the situation and participants.
